CONFIDENTIAL INTERMEDIARY SEARCH — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Sacramento County

DECLARATION OF PURPOSE — CONFIDENTIAL INTERMEDIARY SEARCH INFORMATION SHEET
This Confidential Intermediary Search — Information Sheet describes the statutory mechanism under California Family Code Division 13, Part 2, Chapter 7 (Disclosure of Information, §§ 9200–9209) by which Jordan Lee, as an adoptee or the sibling of an adoptee, may petition the California superior court for Sacramento County to appoint a confidential intermediary to attempt to locate and, without disclosing the underlying sealed adoption records, seek the consent of Casey Alex to contact or an exchange of identifying information. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition contemplated for filing in that court.

As codified in Family Code § 9205, California's confidential-intermediary petition mechanism applies specifically to a search between an adoptee and that adoptee's biological, half-, or step-sibling. It is a narrower, court-supervised alternative that operates only where no mutual waiver is already on file; where an adoptee and a sibling, or an adult adoptee and a birth parent, have both already filed written consent with the California Department of Social Services or a licensed adoption agency, disclosure or contact between them may instead proceed directly under Family Code §§ 9203–9204 without any court petition or confidential intermediary. This information sheet is not itself a court filing and does not itself locate, contact, or obtain the consent of any person.

WHO MAY PETITION FOR A CONFIDENTIAL INTERMEDIARY
California's confidential-intermediary petition mechanism is codified within Family Code § 9205, a section otherwise governing the release of sibling identifying information upon mutual waiver. Family Code § 9205(g) provides that, "[n]otwithstanding subdivisions (a) and (e), an adoptee or sibling who seeks contact with the other for whom no waiver is on file may petition the court to appoint a confidential intermediary." The statute defines "sibling," for these purposes, in § 9205(h): "For purposes of this section, 'sibling' means a biological sibling, half-sibling, or step-sibling of the adoptee." Once such a petition is filed, § 9205(g) further provides that "[t]he court shall grant the petition unless it finds that it would be detrimental to the adoptee or sibling with whom contact is sought."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "an adoptee or sibling who seeks contact with the other for whom no waiver is on file may petition the court to appoint a confidential intermediary"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9205(g) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9205(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9205.)
  "The court shall grant the petition unless it finds that it would be detrimental to the adoptee or sibling with whom contact is sought."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9205(g) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9205(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9205.)
  "For purposes of this section, “sibling” means a biological sibling, half-sibling, or step-sibling of the adoptee."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9205(h) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9205(h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9205.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what Family Code § 9205 itself provides about who may petition for a confidential intermediary; it does not address any other California statute, does not describe the separate, non-petition, mutual-consent disclosure procedures for an adult adoptee and a birth parent found in Family Code §§ 9203–9204 (addressed in a separate clause of this document), and does not determine that any specific petitioner named in this document's companion clauses is eligible to petition under § 9205(g) or that any petition would be granted. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same subdivision, § 9205(g), of a single statutory section, together with the definition in § 9205(h) of the same section; they are treated here as one statutory source, not multiple independent sources. This document is informational only and does not itself file any petition.

WHO SERVES AS THE CONFIDENTIAL INTERMEDIARY
Family Code § 9205(g) does not leave the identity of the confidential intermediary to the petitioner's choice; it assigns the role by statute according to who is sought. Where the person being sought is the adoptee, the statute provides that "the intermediary shall be the department, county adoption agency, or licensed adoption agency that provided adoption services as described in Section 8521 or 8533." Where the agency that conducted the adoption cannot serve, § 9205(g) provides a fallback: "[i]f the court finds that the agency that conducted the adoptee's adoption is unable, due to economic hardship, to serve as the intermediary, then the agency shall provide all records related to the adoptee or the sibling to the court and the court shall appoint an alternate confidential intermediary."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If the sibling being sought is the adoptee, the intermediary shall be the department, county adoption agency, or licensed adoption agency that provided adoption services as described in Section 8521 or 8533."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9205(g) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9205(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9205.)
  "If the court finds that the agency that conducted the adoptee’s adoption is unable, due to economic hardship, to serve as the intermediary, then the agency shall provide all records related to the adoptee or the sibling to the court and the court shall appoint an alternate confidential intermediary."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9205(g) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9205(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9205.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what Family Code § 9205(g) itself provides about who serves as confidential intermediary; it does not restate the separate rule in the same subdivision for a sought sibling who was formerly under juvenile court jurisdiction but is not an adoptee, and it does not identify who would in fact be appointed in any specific case. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same subdivision, § 9205(g), of a single statutory section and are treated here as one statutory source, not multiple independent sources. This document is informational only and does not itself appoint, or predict the appointment of, any confidential intermediary.

WHAT A CONFIDENTIAL INTERMEDIARY DOES — SEARCH, ACCESS, AND THE CONSENT REQUIREMENT
Once appointed under Family Code § 9205(g), a confidential intermediary is given statutory access to otherwise-sealed material for the specific purpose of locating the sought person and asking whether that person consents to disclosure or contact — access the petitioner does not receive directly. The statute provides: "The intermediary shall have access to all records of the adoptee or the sibling and shall make all reasonable efforts to locate and attempt to obtain the consent of the adoptee, sibling, or adoptive or birth parent, as required to make the disclosure authorized by this section." The statute also requires the intermediary to make clear, once the sought person is located, that responding is voluntary: "The confidential intermediary shall notify any located adoptee, sibling, or adoptive or birth parent that consent is optional, not required by law, and does not affect the status of the adoption. If that individual denies the request for consent, the confidential intermediary shall not make any further attempts to obtain consent."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The intermediary shall have access to all records of the adoptee or the sibling and shall make all reasonable efforts to locate and attempt to obtain the consent of the adoptee, sibling, or adoptive or birth parent, as required to make the disclosure authorized by this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9205(g) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9205(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9205.)
  "The confidential intermediary shall notify any located adoptee, sibling, or adoptive or birth parent that consent is optional, not required by law, and does not affect the status of the adoption. If that individual denies the request for consent, the confidential intermediary shall not make any further attempts to obtain consent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9205(g) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9205(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9205.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what Family Code § 9205(g) itself provides about the confidential intermediary's search-and-consent function; it does not restate the section's separate provisions addressing a sought person under 18 years of age, a sought person under juvenile court jurisdiction, or a foreign-born adoptee subject to an intercountry adoption, each of which carries its own statutory rule within the same subdivision. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same subdivision, § 9205(g), of a single statutory section and are treated here as one statutory source, not multiple independent sources. This document is informational only and does not itself conduct, or report the outcome of, any search.

THE CONFIDENTIALITY PROTECTION — WHAT STAYS SEALED AND THE LIMITS ON THE INTERMEDIARY'S OWN USE OF RECORDS
California's adoption records are, as a baseline, closed to the parties themselves: Family Code § 9200(a) provides that the petition, consent, agreement, court order, and investigating agency's report filed in an adoption proceeding are "not open to inspection by any person other than the parties to the proceeding and their attorneys and the department, except upon the written authority of the judge of the superior court." The confidential-intermediary mechanism in § 9205(g) does not repeal that baseline for the petitioner; it instead gives the appointed intermediary — not the petitioner — access to the records, and separately restricts what the intermediary may do with what is found: "The confidential intermediary shall use information found in the records of the adoptee or the sibling for authorized purposes only, and may not disclose that information without authorization." If the sought person is located but does not consent, the statute requires the search to stop rather than the records to be released: "the confidential intermediary shall not make any further attempts to obtain consent."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "is not open to inspection by any person other than the parties to the proceeding and their attorneys and the department, except upon the written authority of the judge of the superior court"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9200(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9200(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9200.)
  "The confidential intermediary shall use information found in the records of the adoptee or the sibling for authorized purposes only, and may not disclose that information without authorization."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9205(g) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9205(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9205.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what Family Code §§ 9200(a) and 9205(g) themselves provide about record confidentiality and the intermediary's own duty of nondisclosure; it does not address every exception to § 9200's general sealing rule (for example, the certificate-of-adoption provision in § 9200(c)), and it does not state what, if any, information a court might independently order disclosed under § 9200(a)'s "good cause approaching the necessitous" standard. The § 9200(a) and § 9205(g) quotations are from two separate, independently numbered statutory sections and are treated as two independent sources; the two § 9205(g) quotations are from the same subdivision and are treated as one source, not two. This document is informational only and does not itself disclose any sealed adoption record.

DISTINCTION FROM THE SEPARATE MUTUAL-CONSENT DISCLOSURE PROCEDURE FOR ADULT ADOPTEES AND BIRTH PARENTS
California law places the court-petition confidential-intermediary mechanism of Family Code § 9205(g) alongside a structurally different, non-petition mechanism in the same chapter for an adult adoptee and a birth parent. Family Code § 9203(a)(1) provides that the department or a licensed adoption agency shall, "[u]pon the request of a person who has been adopted pursuant to this part and who has attained 21 years of age, disclose the identity of the person's birth parent or parents and their most current address shown in the records of the department or licensed adoption agency, if the birth parent or parents have indicated consent to the disclosure in writing." Family Code § 9204(a) similarly provides that, "[n]otwithstanding any other law, if an adult adoptee and the adult adoptee's birth parents have each filed a written consent with the department or licensed adoption agency, the department or licensed adoption agency may arrange for contact between those persons. Neither the department nor a licensed adoption agency may solicit, directly or indirectly, the execution of a written consent." Unlike § 9205(g)'s confidential-intermediary petition, neither § 9203 nor § 9204 involves a court petition, a court-appointed intermediary, or an intermediary's search of sealed records for a person who has not already come forward; both instead operate only after each side has independently filed a written consent or waiver with the department or agency.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Upon the request of a person who has been adopted pursuant to this part and who has attained 21 years of age, disclose the identity of the person’s birth parent or parents and their most current address shown in the records of the department or licensed adoption agency, if the birth parent or parents have indicated consent to the disclosure in writing."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9203(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9203(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9203.)
  "Notwithstanding any other law, if an adult adoptee and the adult adoptee’s birth parents have each filed a written consent with the department or licensed adoption agency, the department or licensed adoption agency may arrange for contact between those persons. Neither the department nor a licensed adoption agency may solicit, directly or indirectly, the execution of a written consent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9204(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9204(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9204.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what Family Code §§ 9203(a)(1) and 9204(a) themselves provide about the mutual-consent disclosure and contact procedure, as a point of statutory contrast with the § 9205(g) confidential-intermediary petition described in this document's companion clauses; it does not restate § 9203's remaining subdivisions (including the separate procedure for an adoptive parent's request under § 9203(a)(3), fee provisions, or the January 1, 1984 applicability date in § 9203(g)), and it does not address adoptions to which § 9203 does not apply. The § 9203(a)(1) and § 9204(a) quotations are from two separate, independently numbered statutory sections and are treated as two independent sources. This document is informational only and does not itself file any consent, waiver, or request with the department or any adoption agency.

DECLARATION AND SIGNATURE — CONFIDENTIAL INTERMEDIARY SEARCH INFORMATION SHEET
